info.name: PayMesh API
info.description:
PayMesh Payment-as-a-Service API.

Set `baseUrl` (defaults to http://localhost:8080). Run the folders top to bottom: onboarding creates a merchant, Identity & Auth attaches a user and captures a token, and Authenticated access uses it.

Capabilities covered: Identity & Auth, Merchant, Customer, Order, Payment Intents, and the shared transactional outbox (ADR-010).

item.name: Merchant (public onboarding)
item.description: Creating a merchant is the signup step and needs no token -- it precedes having an account at all. Reading one does need a token; those requests live in 'Authenticated access' below, after a session exists.

request.description: Input is deliberately untrimmed and mixed-case: the domain trims the business name, lowercases the email, and uppercases country and currency.

exec: // Unique email per run so the unique constraint does not fail a repeat run.

request.description: Reuses the email from 'Register merchant'. Run that request first.
Bean Validation failure: returns VALIDATION_FAILED with a populated fieldErrors map.
Domain invariant failure, which Bean Validation cannot express: returns INVALID_REQUEST with an empty fieldErrors map.

exec: pm.test('names the broken rule', () => pm.expect(body.message).to.eql('Country must be of length 2'));

item.name: Identity & Auth
item.description:
Registration, login, and rotating refresh tokens.

Run the requests in order: each depends on tokens captured by the previous one. The reuse request deliberately revokes the whole family, so re-run from 'Register user' to get a working session again.

request.description: Attaches the user to the merchant registered above, granting MERCHANT_ADMIN scoped to it. That scope is what every request in 'Authenticated access' relies on.

exec: pm.test('scoped to the merchant just created', () => pm.expect(b.roles[0].merchantId).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('merchantId')));
pm.test('access token is a three-part JWT', () => pm.expect(b.accessToken.split('.')).to.have.lengthOf(3));
pm.test('refresh token is opaque, not a JWT', () => pm.expect(b.refreshToken.split('.')).to.have.lengthOf(1));

request.description: The body here must be byte-identical to the unknown-email response below: a difference would let an attacker enumerate registered addresses.

exec: pm.test('response is indistinguishable from a wrong password', () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('wrongPasswordBody')));

request.description: Spending a refresh token revokes it and mints a successor in the same family.

exec: pm.test('a new refresh token was issued', () => pm.expect(b.refreshToken).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('refreshToken')));

item.name: Refresh - reuse a spent token (401, revokes the family)

request.description: Presenting an already-spent token means it leaked. There is no way to tell the thief from the victim, so the entire family is revoked and both are forced back through login. The next request proves the live successor died with it.
This token was valid a moment ago. Reuse detection revoked the whole lineage.
Idempotent: an unknown or already-revoked token is a silent no-op, so logout cannot be used to probe whether a token is still live.

item.name: Authenticated access
item.description:
Everything that requires a bearer token. Run 'Merchant (public onboarding)' and 'Identity & Auth' first -- these use the access token captured by Login.

The cross-tenant requests build a second, unrelated merchant and user to prove that one tenant cannot see another's data.

request.description: Reading a merchant is not public, even though creating one is.
A structurally valid JWT carrying the right claims but signed with the wrong key. The filter chain verifies the signature, so claims alone buy nothing.
There is no merchantId field in this body. The tenant comes from the token, which is what makes writing under someone else's merchant impossible rather than merely discouraged.

exec: pm.test('lookup hashes are never exposed', () => { const s = JSON.stringify(b); pm.expect(s).to.not.include('emailHash'); pm.expect(s).to.not.include('phoneHash'); });

request.description: Unique per merchant, not globally.

item.name: Cross-tenant setup: register a second merchant

request.description: Answering 403 would confirm the id is real, turning this endpoint into an oracle for enumerating tenants. It is reported as not found instead.
Same rule one level down: an id alone never authorizes a read.
The reference that just returned 409 for the first merchant is available here, because uniqueness is scoped to the tenant.

item.name: Orders
item.description: Runs after Authenticated access, which captured accessToken, customerId and otherAccessToken. Covers both writes behind the idempotency layer, cursor pagination, and the cross-tenant 404.

item.name: Setup: a customer under the second merchant

request.description: Belongs to the SECOND merchant. Used below to prove that naming another tenant's customer on an order is rejected without confirming the customer is real.
There is no merchantId in this body. The tenant comes from the token. Money is an integer count of minor units with the currency in its own field.

exec: pm.test('amount is an integer of minor units', () => { pm.expect(b.amountMinor).to.eql(1999); pm.expect(Number.isInteger(b.amountMinor)).to.be.true; });

item.name: Create order - replay the same key and body (idempotent)

request.description: A network retry. Same key, same body: the stored response comes back verbatim and the handler never runs again.

exec: pm.test('201 Created, replayed not re-executed', () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));

item.name: Create order - same key, different body (409)

request.description: The key was already used for a different request. Replaying the first answer would be a lie, so this is refused rather than served from the record.
The header is mandatory on this route: a write that can create money movement must be safe to retry.

A FRESH Idempotency-Key, so this is a genuinely new request -- and it still hits the unique constraint. The two de-duplication rules are independent: the header answers 'same request?', the reference answers 'same purchase?'.

item.name: Create order - linked to a customer of this merchant (201)
Create order - customer of another merchant (422, reveals nothing)

request.description: The customer is real; it belongs to the other merchant. The next request proves the answer is identical to one for a customer that never existed, so this endpoint cannot be used to confirm another tenant's customer ids.

item.name: Create order - customer that never existed (422, identical answer)
Cross-tenant: read another merchant's order (404, not 403)

request.description: A real order id and a valid token for a different merchant. 403 would confirm the id exists and turn this route into an oracle for enumerating other tenants' orders.

exec: pm.test('collection envelope, not a bare array', () => { pm.expect(b).to.have.property('data'); pm.expect(b.data).to.be.an('array'); pm.expect(b).to.have.property('pagination'); });
pm.test('every order belongs to the caller', () => b.data.forEach(o => pm.expect(o.merchantId).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('merchantId'))));
pm.test('the created orders are listed', () => pm.expect(b.data.map(o => o.id)).to.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('orderId')));

item.name: List orders - first page of one (200, captures the cursor)
List orders - second page via the cursor (200, no repeats)

request.description: Keyset pagination over (created_at, order_id). The order id is the tiebreak: without it, two orders created in the same instant would be skipped or repeated at a page boundary.

exec: pm.test('a different order than page one', () => pm.expect(b.data[0].id).to.not.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('firstPageId')));

item.name: List orders - limit above the cap (200, capped at 100)

exec: pm.test('no internal type names in the message', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.not.include('enum'));

item.name: Cross-tenant: list orders sees none of them (200, empty)

exec: pm.test('the other merchant has no orders', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().data.length).to.eql(0));

request.description: Cancelling is a write, so the tenant check matters more here than on a read. Still 404, not 403.
Cancellation is requested as an action. There is no status field to set: the aggregate owns the state machine.

item.name: Cancel again on a FRESH key (409)

request.description: A new key means a new request, so it reaches the state machine -- which refuses, because the order is no longer PENDING.

item.name: Cancel again on the SAME key (200, replayed)

request.description: The same request as the one that succeeded. It never reaches the state machine, so it gets the stored 200 rather than the 409 above.

exec: pm.test('the cancelled order is there', () => pm.expect(b.data.map(o => o.id)).to.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('orderId')));

item.name: Outbox (order.created)
item.description:
The outbox has no HTTP surface, and that is deliberate: outbox_events is internal platform state that a relay will read, never a resource a merchant can fetch. What can be asserted from outside is the boundary itself -- an order and its order.created event commit together, so an order that is readable proves its event was written, and a create that was refused proves neither row landed.

The rollback half of the invariant cannot be reached over HTTP (nothing makes the outbox insert fail on demand); it is proved in OutboxTransactionIntegrationTest.leavesNoOrderRowBehindWhenTheOutboxAppendFails. See ADR-010.

Runs top to bottom and depends on the Identity & Auth folder having captured accessToken.

item.name: Create an order (order + order.created, one transaction)

request.description: One call, two rows: the order and its order.created event, in a single database transaction (ADR-010). Only the order is visible here.

exec: pm.test('the outbox stays internal: no event fields on the resource', () => {

item.name: The order is readable, so its event committed with it (200)

request.description: The two writes share one commit, so a readable order is proof the event row is there too. If the outbox insert had failed, this would be a 404 -- the order would have rolled back with it.

exec: pm.test('amount survived the commit intact', () => pm.expect(b.amountMinor).to.eql(4200));
pm.test('still PENDING: nothing consumes order.created yet', () => pm.expect(b.status).to.eql('PENDING'));

request.description: A FRESH Idempotency-Key, so this is a genuinely new request. It is refused before the transaction opens, so neither an order row nor an event row is written -- the next request counts what actually landed.

item.name: Exactly one order carries the reference (200)

request.description: The observable half of 'both or neither': the refused create left no partial order behind, so the reference appears exactly once.

exec: pm.test('one order, not two, not zero', () => pm.expect(matches).to.have.lengthOf(1));
pm.test('and it is the one that was created', () => pm.expect(matches[0].id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('outboxOrderId')));

item.name: Payment Intents
item.description:
Runs after Orders, which captured accessToken, customerId, otherAccessToken and linkedOrderId -- a 2500 INR order of the first merchant that is still PENDING.

An order says what is owed; an intent says how it is being collected. The intent is operational state, not the financial record: nothing here moves a balance, and the Ledger that will is not built.

The subject of this folder is ADR-011. An order holds AT MOST ONE live intent, and it is a partial unique index that enforces it -- the application's pre-check exists only for the friendlier message and is never trusted. Cancelling is how the slot is released.

request.description: No merchantId and no status in the body: the tenant comes from the token and the state machine owns the state. The amount must be the order's EXACTLY -- one live intent for the whole obligation is what makes overpayment structurally impossible rather than merely check-constrained.

exec: pm.test('amount is the order amount, in minor units', () => { pm.expect(b.amountMinor).to.eql(2500); pm.expect(Number.isInteger(b.amountMinor)).to.be.true; });

pm.test('NO clientSecret -- a credential nothing can verify is not issued', () => { pm.expect(b).to.not.have.property('clientSecret'); pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.not.include('clientSecret'); });

item.name: Create a second intent for the same order (409)

request.description: A FRESH Idempotency-Key, so this is a genuinely new request and reaches the create path. The order already holds a live intent and uq_payment_intents_live_per_order says it may hold only one (ADR-011). Retrying this will never succeed: the way forward is to cancel the live intent, which is what the last requests in this folder do.

item.name: Create - amount is not the order's (422)

request.description: 422, not 400: nothing about the request is malformed, the amount simply is not the order's. An intent collects its order's exact obligation, so there is no partial and no over-collection to argue about.

exec: pm.test('checked before the live-intent slot, so this is not reported as a 409', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.not.eql(409));

item.name: Cross-tenant: create against another merchant's order (422)

request.description: A real order id and a valid token for a different merchant. ORDER_NOT_PAYABLE is ONE code for three causes -- no such order, not this merchant's order, order not PENDING -- because splitting them would turn this endpoint into an oracle for enumerating another tenant's order ids.

exec: pm.test('not a 409 -- the other merchant is not told the order has a live intent', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.not.eql(409));
pm.test('amount and currency unchanged since creation', () => { pm.expect(b.amountMinor).to.eql(2500); pm.expect(b.currency).to.eql('INR'); });
pm.test('still no clientSecret on a read either', () => pm.expect(b).to.not.have.property('clientSecret'));

item.name: Cross-tenant: read another merchant's intent (404, not 403)

request.description: A pi_ in a path authorizes nothing. 403 would confirm the intent exists; 404 says only that this merchant has no such intent.

exec: pm.test('collection envelope, not a bare array', () => { pm.expect(b).to.have.property('data'); pm.expect(b.data).to.be.an('array'); pm.expect(b).to.have.property('pagination'); });
pm.test('every intent belongs to the caller', () => b.data.forEach(i => pm.expect(i.merchantId).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('merchantId'))));
pm.test('the created intent is listed', () => pm.expect(b.data.map(i => i.id)).to.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('paymentIntentId')));
pm.test('the refused creates left nothing behind', () => pm.expect(b.data.filter(i => i.orderId === pm.collectionVariables.get('linkedOrderId'))).to.have.lengthOf(1));

request.description: Which intents does this order have? Exactly one, and that is ADR-011 observable.

exec: pm.test('the created intent is there', () => pm.expect(b.data.map(i => i.id)).to.include(pm.collectionVariables.get('paymentIntentId')));
pm.test('one live intent per order', () => pm.expect(b.data).to.have.lengthOf(1));

item.name: List - filter by a status nothing has reached (200, empty)

request.description: SUCCEEDED is declared in the status CHECK from V8 but no transition reaches it yet -- the provider callbacks that would are a later PR. An empty data array is the whole point: the filter is honoured, and the state is genuinely unreachable today.

exec: pm.test('a known status is accepted, not rejected', () => pm.expect(pm.response.code).to.not.eql(400));
pm.test('the envelope is still an envelope', () => { pm.expect(b.pagination.hasMore).to.eql(false); pm.expect(b.pagination.nextCursor).to.be.oneOf([null, undefined]); });

request.description: Cancellation is requested as an action; there is no status field to set. It is also the only way the order's live-intent slot is released (ADR-011), which is why every state a customer can strand an intent in has a merchant cancel route -- except PROCESSING, deliberately, because an in-flight attempt may already have succeeded at the provider.

exec: pm.test('same intent, not a new one', () => pm.expect(b.id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('paymentIntentId')));

item.name: Cancel again on a FRESH key (409)

request.description: A new key means a new request, so it reaches the state machine -- which refuses, because CANCELLED is terminal.

The header is mandatory on this route. Rejected by the idempotency filter before the handler runs, so nothing is created -- note the order's slot is free at this point and this create would otherwise have succeeded.

exec: pm.test('refused before the handler, so no intent came back', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.not.have.property('id'));

item.name: Payment Intents - attach, confirm and the ADR-013 guard
Setup: an order to attach and confirm against (201)

request.description: Its own order, because the intents earlier in this collection have already been cancelled and an order holds at most one live intent (ADR-011).

item.name: Setup: a payment intent for it (201)

request.description: Starts at REQUIRES_PAYMENT_METHOD with no payment method: paymentMethodType is null until one is attached, and nothing defaults it.

exec: pm.test('no method until one is attached', () => pm.expect(b.paymentMethodType).to.be.oneOf([null, undefined]));

request.description: Attach is a genuine prerequisite, not a convention. An intent with no instrument has nothing to be collected with, and inferring a default would pick one on the merchant's behalf.

A method TYPE, not a token. payment_method_tokens exists (V3) and nothing can write to it until the Provider Simulator does, so requiring a token would make this endpoint uncallable. No PAN, no expiry, no holder name reaches PayMesh (SDD 12.6).

exec: pm.test('no instrument data echoed back', () => { const t = pm.response.text(); pm.expect(t).to.not.include('token'); pm.expect(t).to.not.include('pan'); });

item.name: Attach again on the SAME key (200, replayed)

request.description: The same key never reaches the state machine at all: the stored response comes back, byte for byte, with Idempotency-Replayed: true.

item.name: Attach again on a FRESH key (409)

request.description: A genuinely new request, so it meets the state machine. Re-attaching is refused rather than quietly allowed: past this point an attempt may be in flight, and a stored method that disagrees with what the provider was asked for is worse than none. Cancel and start again.
CARD, UPI, NET_BANKING or WALLET. Refused at the boundary, and the error names the field rather than a Java type.

202 AND NOT 200, even though nothing asynchronous is invoked: the intent is PROCESSING and the outcome is undecided until a provider callback resolves it. There is no outbound call anywhere in Payment yet. The returnUrl's query string is stripped before it is stored on the attempt -- it routinely carries a session token and that row is a durable audit record.

exec: pm.test('202 Accepted -- the work is started, not finished', () => pm.response.to.have.status(202));
pm.test('confirming captures nothing -- the Ledger is not involved', () => { pm.expect(b.capturedAmountMinor).to.eql(0); pm.expect(b.refundedAmountMinor).to.eql(0); });
pm.test('same intent, not a new one', () => pm.expect(b.id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('confirmIntentId')));

item.name: Confirm again on the SAME key (202, replayed)

request.description: A network retry must cost nothing -- and must not open a second attempt against the same intent.

item.name: Confirm again on a FRESH key (409)

request.description: A genuinely new request meets the state machine, which refuses it: PROCESSING is not confirmable.

THE ONE STATE WITH NO CANCEL, and it is a named deferral rather than an oversight (ADR-011 section 5). An in-flight attempt may already have succeeded at the provider, so cancelling locally could erase a payment that really happened -- money taken from a customer with no record of it here, which is strictly worse than a stuck order. The full answer is a PROCESSING timeout plus provider reconciliation, and neither is in scope.
For the ADR-013 walkthrough below: an order that will be cancelled out from under a live intent.

item.name: Setup: an intent for it, with a method attached (200)

request.description: Created while the order was payable, which is the only time Payment used to check.

item.name: Setup: attach a method to it (200)

request.description: Attach is not guarded by the order re-read: it commits PayMesh to nothing.

item.name: Cancel the ORDER out from under the live intent (200)

request.description: Nothing stops this, and nothing should: Order.cancel checks only that the order is PENDING and must never learn that Payment exists (design section 0.5). The order is now CANCELLED with a live intent still attached to it.

ADR-013, AND THE MOST IMPORTANT REQUEST IN THIS FOLDER. Confirm re-reads the order's payability inside its own transaction and refuses. Without it PayMesh would collect for an order the merchant explicitly cancelled. ORDER_NOT_PAYABLE is one code for three causes -- no such order, not yours, not payable -- because splitting them would let a caller enumerate another tenant's order ids.

The route out of REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION, new in this PR (ADR-011's slot-release table). Without it an abandoned checkout would hold the order's only slot forever, and a stuck intent is a stuck order. The method it died holding is kept, not cleared.

exec: pm.test('the method it died holding is kept', () => pm.expect(b.paymentMethodType).to.eql('UPI'));

request.description: Both new writes are registered in IdempotencyConfiguration.IDEMPOTENT_ROUTES as path templates, so both require the header.
Same registry, same answer.

item.name: Provider callbacks (internal, HMAC-signed)
item.description: POST /internal/v1/provider-callbacks/{provider}. NOT the merchant surface: no bearer token, not under /api/, and deliberately not idempotency-keyed -- provider_callbacks is its deduplication (ADR-012). Every request here signs its own body in a pre-request script; there is no fixed signature to paste, because a signature is valid for one body at one second.

request.description: Its own order: an order holds at most one live payment intent (ADR-011), and every intent earlier in this collection has already claimed one.

item.name: Setup: a payment intent for it (201)

request.description: REQUIRES_PAYMENT_METHOD. Nothing a provider says can reach it yet.
REQUIRES_CONFIRMATION.
PROCESSING, with one attempt open. 202 because the outcome is genuinely undecided until a callback resolves it -- which is what the rest of this folder does.

exec: // A fixed base instant for the ordering demonstrations below, so 'earlier' and 'later' are
// facts about the provider's clock rather than about how fast this collection runs.

request.description: The HMAC is the authentication. There is no bearer token on this route and no other credential to fall back to.

exec: // THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED HERE, NOT PASTED. A fixed signature would be valid for one
// body at one second and would rot the moment either changed -- which is the property the
// scheme exists to have, so hard-coding one would be testing nothing.

const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: 'sim_evt_' + pm.variables.replaceIn('{{$guid}}'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbOccurredAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'SUCCEEDED', capturedAmountMinor: 2500 });
// The signed string is t + '.' + body, so a captured signature cannot be replayed onto a
// different body or a different time. HMAC-SHA256, hex, with the shared secret.
// The request body is literally {{callbackBody}}, so what is sent is byte-for-byte what
// was signed. Building the JSON in the request pane instead would sign one string and
// send another the first time a variable resolved differently.
pm.test('says nothing about which check failed', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().code).to.eql('PROVIDER_SIGNATURE_INVALID'));

item.name: Callback signed over a different body (401)

request.description: The body is inside the signed string, so a captured signature cannot be pasted onto a new body. Otherwise anyone who ever saw one callback could mark any payment succeeded.

exec: // THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED HERE, NOT PASTED. A fixed signature would be valid for one
// body at one second and would rot the moment either changed -- which is the property the
// scheme exists to have, so hard-coding one would be testing nothing.

const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: 'sim_evt_' + pm.variables.replaceIn('{{$guid}}'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbOccurredAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'SUCCEEDED', capturedAmountMinor: 2500 });
// The signed string is t + '.' + body, so a captured signature cannot be replayed onto a
// different body or a different time. HMAC-SHA256, hex, with the shared secret.
// The request body is literally {{callbackBody}}, so what is sent is byte-for-byte what
// was signed. Building the JSON in the request pane instead would sign one string and
// send another the first time a variable resolved differently.
// Sign one body, then send a different one.

request.description: The timestamp is signed, not merely sent, so it cannot be rewritten to refresh a captured signature. Anything more than 300 seconds out, in either direction, is refused.

exec: const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: 'sim_evt_' + pm.variables.replaceIn('{{$guid}}'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbOccurredAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'SUCCEEDED', capturedAmountMinor: 2500 });
// A perfectly valid signature, stamped 400 seconds ago.

request.description: The customer has a 3DS challenge to complete. The action URL is stored REDACTED -- origin and path survive, the query string does not, because it carries a challenge token.

exec: // THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED HERE, NOT PASTED. A fixed signature would be valid for one
// body at one second and would rot the moment either changed -- which is the property the
// scheme exists to have, so hard-coding one would be testing nothing.

const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: 'sim_evt_' + pm.variables.replaceIn('{{$guid}}'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbOccurredAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'REQUIRES_ACTION', actionUrl: 'https://3ds.simulator.test/challenge/abc?token=SECRET' });
// The signed string is t + '.' + body, so a captured signature cannot be replayed onto a
// different body or a different time. HMAC-SHA256, hex, with the shared secret.
// The request body is literally {{callbackBody}}, so what is sent is byte-for-byte what
// was signed. Building the JSON in the request pane instead would sign one string and
// send another the first time a variable resolved differently.
// Kept so the next two requests can re-deliver this exact event.

request.description: A provider retries whether the response was lost or never sent. The row loses on pk_provider_callbacks, the transaction rolls back, and nothing happened -- no transition, no state-history row, no outbox event. 200 and never 409: a conflict here is an infinite retry loop.

exec: // THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED HERE, NOT PASTED. A fixed signature would be valid for one
// body at one second and would rot the moment either changed -- which is the property the
// scheme exists to have, so hard-coding one would be testing nothing.

const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbChallengeEventId'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbOccurredAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'REQUIRES_ACTION', actionUrl: 'https://3ds.simulator.test/challenge/abc?token=SECRET' });
// The signed string is t + '.' + body, so a captured signature cannot be replayed onto a
// different body or a different time. HMAC-SHA256, hex, with the shared secret.
// The request body is literally {{callbackBody}}, so what is sent is byte-for-byte what
// was signed. Building the JSON in the request pane instead would sign one string and
// send another the first time a variable resolved differently.

request.description: REQUIRES_ACTION back to PROCESSING, opening a second attempt. THIS IS THE CYCLE the monotonic event clock exists for: inside it a stale REQUIRES_ACTION is a LEGAL transition, so the state machine alone cannot refuse it.

item.name: A stale REQUIRES_ACTION arriving late (200, IGNORED_STALE)

request.description: Its occurredAt is earlier than the event already applied, and the transition it asks for is legal. Only last_provider_event_at refuses it -- read as the maximum across the intent attempts, because the re-confirm above opened a new one whose own clock is null.

exec: // THE SIGNATURE IS COMPUTED HERE, NOT PASTED. A fixed signature would be valid for one
// body at one second and would rot the moment either changed -- which is the property the
// scheme exists to have, so hard-coding one would be testing nothing.

const body = JSON.stringify({ eventId: 'sim_evt_' + pm.variables.replaceIn('{{$guid}}'), occurredAt: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbEarlierAt'), paymentIntentId: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbIntentId'), providerReference: pm.collectionVariables.get('cbReference'), outcome: 'REQUIRES_ACTION', actionUrl: 'https://3ds.simulator.test/challenge/abc' });
// The signed string is t + '.' + body, so a captured signature cannot be replayed onto a
// different body or a different time. HMAC-SHA256, hex, with the shared secret.
// The request body is literally {{callbackBody}}, so what is sent is byte-for-byte what
// was signed. Building the JSON in the request pane instead would sign one string and
// send another the first time a variable resolved differently.

item.name: Payment Intents - manual capture
item.description:
AUTHORIZED -> SUCCEEDED at the merchant's request, and AUTHORIZED -> CANCELLED when they decide against it (design spec 5, ADR-011). Runs top to bottom and depends on the earlier folders for {{accessToken}}, {{otherAccessToken}} and {{providerCallbackSecret}}.

Reaching AUTHORIZED needs a provider callback, because only a provider can authorize -- so two requests here are HMAC-signed against the internal endpoint, with the signature computed in a pre-request script rather than pasted.

This folder completes the intent state machine: after it every status is reachable except PARTIALLY_REFUNDED and REFUNDED, which belong to the Refund capability.

item.name: Event delivery (outbox relay to order.PAID)
item.description:
THE LOOP THAT DID NOT CLOSE UNTIL ADR-016: create an order, collect against it, and watch the ORDER reach PAID without anyone calling an order endpoint.

Payment writes payment.succeeded to outbox_events in the same transaction as the payment (ADR-010). The relay reads it, the dispatcher hands it to Order's consumer, and Order moves its own status and amountPaidMinor. Payment still never writes the orders table, which is why ModuleBoundaryTest.orderNeverImportsPayment keeps an empty allowlist.

START THE APP WITH THE RELAY ON:
    PAYMESH_EVENTS_OUTBOX_RELAY_ENABLED=true ./mvnw spring-boot:run
The dev profile that spring-boot:run activates switches the relay OFF, because that same profile is what the test suite runs under and a timer moving orders to PAID mid-assertion is a flake generator. Without the variable, the last request here polls ten times and fails.

Runs after the folders above and reuses their access token; it mints its own order, intent and idempotency keys, so it disturbs nothing they left behind.

item.name: Provider Simulator (/sim/v1, ADR-017)
item.description:
THE PROVIDER, NOT THE MERCHANT API. Everything here is under /sim/v1 and none of it is part of the surface a merchant integrates against.

Authentication is X-PayMesh-Simulator-Key and nothing else -- not a bearer token, which is refused on purpose: these routes queue the callback that marks a payment SUCCEEDED, so a merchant able to call them could authorize their own collection (ADR-017 section 3).

The first eighteen requests need no background job and run against a plain `./mvnw spring-boot:run`. The last six drive a real payment intent end to end and need the callback dispatcher, which the dev profile switches OFF so it cannot mutate rows under a test. Start the server with PAYMESH_SIMULATOR_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true for those.

Depends on Identity & Auth having captured {{accessToken}}, like every other folder here.

request.description: The only authentication on /sim/v1/** is X-PayMesh-Simulator-Key. This route queues a callback that marks a payment SUCCEEDED, so an unauthenticated simulator would be an unauthenticated way to collect any payment on the platform (ADR-017 section 3).

request.description: THE ONE THAT MATTERS. A merchant able to drive the provider could authorize their own collection. The chain permits the route -- there is no bearer token to evaluate -- and the filter refuses it anyway, because a token is not one of the ways to produce the key.

item.name: Ledger (a payment becomes a balance, ADR-018)
item.description:
WHERE THE MONEY IS ACTUALLY WRITTEN DOWN. Before ADR-018 a payment reaching SUCCEEDED meant PayMesh held a row saying a payment succeeded -- it did not mean anybody's money had moved, because there was nowhere for money to be.

This folder collects 99900 and watches the merchant's pending balance rise by exactly that. Nothing here calls a ledger endpoint, because there is no way to write to the ledger over HTTP: the only writer is a consumer of payment.succeeded, which means every posting traces back to a committed payment. SDD 15.3's POST /internal/v1/ledger/transactions is deliberately absent (ADR-018 section 3).

Double-entry, so the capture is written twice and the two sides must match:
    DEBIT   provider-clearing:INR        99900   <- the provider owes us
    CREDIT  merchant:<you>:pending:INR   99900   <- we owe the merchant
That rule is enforced by a DEFERRED PostgreSQL trigger checked at COMMIT, not by Java, and so is the immutability of a posted entry. A correction is a new reversal journal, never an edit -- which is what Refund will have to write.

START THE APP WITH BOTH TIMERS ON, or the balance never moves:
    PAYMESH_SIMULATOR_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true \
    PAYMESH_EVENTS_OUTBOX_RELAY_ENABLED=true \
    ./mvnw spring-boot:run

Runs after the folders above and reuses their access token; it mints its own order, intent and idempotency keys, so it disturbs nothing they left behind.

This merchant has been paid by earlier folders, so the figure is usually not zero -- what matters is that it moves by exactly the amount collected below. A merchant who has never been paid gets an empty list here, not a 404: 'you have earned nothing yet' is not an error.

item.name: THE POINT: the balance moves by exactly what was collected (200)

request.description:
THE LINE THIS WHOLE FOLDER EXISTS FOR. Nobody called a ledger endpoint -- there isn't one to call. Payment wrote payment.succeeded, the relay read it, and the Ledger's own consumer posted a balanced journal (ADR-018):

    DEBIT   provider-clearing:INR        99900
    CREDIT  merchant:<you>:pending:INR   99900

The figure below is not a stored column. It is a SUM over the immutable entries, computed when you ask -- so it cannot drift from the journal the way a cached projection could.

IT POLLS, because delivery is asynchronous by design. Two things must both have happened: the simulator's dispatcher must have sent the callback, and the outbox relay must have delivered the event.

REQUIRES BOTH TIMERS ON:
    PAYMESH_SIMULATOR_DISPATCH_ENABLED=true \
    PAYMESH_EVENTS_OUTBOX_RELAY_ENABLED=true \
    ./mvnw spring-boot:run
The dev profile switches both off, because it is the profile the test suite runs under and a timer moving money mid-assertion is a flake generator. Without them this request exhausts its attempts and fails, which is the honest outcome rather than a skip.

request.description:
A balance read is a read. Worth one request because the ledger's idempotency is easy to assume and hard to see: the same payment cannot post twice however many times its event is delivered.

Two independent guards make that true. processed_events (V14) stops one EVENT being applied twice by one consumer. uq_ledger_transactions_idempotency, keyed on 'payment-captured:<intent id>', stops one PAYMENT being posted twice however many events describe it -- a replayed backlog, a renamed consumer, a manual re-run.

Leave the app running and re-run this folder's last two requests as often as you like; the figure does not move again.

item.name: A different merchant sees their own money, never yours (200)

request.description:
TENANT ISOLATION, AND THE REQUEST CANNOT EVEN EXPRESS THE VIOLATION. There is no merchant parameter on this endpoint -- no path variable, no query string, no body. The tenant comes from the verified token, so the only balance a caller can address is their own.

That is why this returns 200 with someone else's (empty or unrelated) figures rather than 403: there is nothing to forbid.

Nothing under /api/v1 is open by accident. The balance endpoint needed no security configuration of its own: everything not explicitly permitted is authenticated, and adding a rule for this route would be a no-op implying the default runs the other way.
